claim: Anti-EGFR therapy-associated cutaneous toxicity is characterized by papulopustular rash, local inflammation, folliculitis, and microbial infection.
source: Anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) therapy–associated cutaneous toxicity is a syndrome characterized by papulopustular rash, local inflammation, folliculitis, and microbial infection, resulting in a decrease in quality of life and dose interruption.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the syndrome.

claim: Anti-EGFR therapy-associated cutaneous toxicity results in a decrease in quality of life and dose interruption.
source: Anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) therapy–associated cutaneous toxicity is a syndrome characterized by papulopustular rash, local inflammation, folliculitis, and microbial infection, resulting in a decrease in quality of life and dose interruption.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a consequence of the syndrome.

claim: No effective clinical intervention is available for anti-EGFR therapy-associated cutaneous toxicity.
source: However, no effective clinical intervention is available for this adverse effect.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in current treatment options.

claim: Atrophy of dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT) correlates with rash occurrence and exacerbation in a murine model of EGFR inhibitor-induced rash.
source: Here, we report the atrophy of dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT), a highly plastic adipose tissue with various skin-specific functions, correlates with rash occurrence and exacerbation in a murine model of EGFR inhibitor-induced rash.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the murine model experiments.

claim: dWAT is a highly plastic adipose tissue with various skin-specific functions.
source: Here, we report the atrophy of dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT), a highly plastic adipose tissue with various skin-specific functions, correlates with rash occurrence and exacerbation in a murine model of EGFR inhibitor-induced rash.
evidence: This is a characterization of dWAT stated in the abstract.

claim: The reduction in dWAT is due to the inhibition of adipogenic differentiation by defects in PPARγ signaling.
source: The reduction in dWAT is due to the inhibition of adipogenic differentiation by defects in peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) signaling, and increased lipolysis by the induced expression of the lipolytic cytokine IL6.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The reduction in dWAT is due to increased lipolysis by the induced expression of the lipolytic cytokine IL6.
source: The reduction in dWAT is due to the inhibition of adipogenic differentiation by defects in peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) signaling, and increased lipolysis by the induced expression of the lipolytic cytokine IL6.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone maintains adipogenic differentiation.
source: The activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone maintains adipogenic differentiation and represses the transcription of IL6, eventually improving skin functions and ameliorating the severity of rash without altering the antitumor effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone represses the transcription of IL6.
source: The activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone maintains adipogenic differentiation and represses the transcription of IL6, eventually improving skin functions and ameliorating the severity of rash without altering the antitumor effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone improves skin functions and ameliorates the severity of rash without altering the antitumor effects.
source: The activation of PPARγ by rosiglitazone maintains adipogenic differentiation and represses the transcription of IL6, eventually improving skin functions and ameliorating the severity of rash without altering the antitumor effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Activation of PPARγ represents a promising approach to ameliorate cutaneous toxicity in patients with cancer who receive anti-EGFR therapy.
source: Thus, activation of PPARγ represents a promising approach to ameliorate cutaneous toxicity in patients with cancer who receive anti-EGFR therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rash is observed in 70–90% of patients receiving anti-EGFR therapy.
source: Most commonly, rash is observed in 70–90% of patients receiving anti-EGFR therapy (Cappuzzo et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2017; Sequist et al., 2013), resulting in a decrease in quality of life.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cutaneous toxicity is responsible for 8–17% of dose modifications and interruptions in anti-EGFR therapy.
source: Except for the empiric use of corticosteroids and antibiotics, no effective clinical treatment is currently available for these adverse effects, which is responsible for 8–17% of dose modifications and interruptions (Lacouture, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Biopsies from rodents with genetic ablation of EGFR or pharmacological EGFR inhibitors showed a dramatic loss of dermal adipose tissue.
source: An analysis of biopsies from rodents with the genetic ablation of EGFR or pharmacological EGFR inhibitors both showed a dramatic loss of dermal adipose tissue (Murillas et al., 1995; Sibilia and Wagner, 1995; Sugawara et al., 2010; Surguladze et al., 2009), a newly recognized adipose layer termed dermal white adipose tissue (dWAT).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Local infection induces dWAT expansion.
source: For example, local infection (Zhang et al., 2015), a high-fat diet (HFD) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) agonists (Zhang et al., 2019a) induce dWAT expansion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A high-fat diet induces dWAT expansion.
source: For example, local infection (Zhang et al., 2015), a high-fat diet (HFD) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) agonists (Zhang et al., 2019a) induce dWAT expansion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PPARγ agonists induce dWAT expansion.
source: For example, local infection (Zhang et al., 2015), a high-fat diet (HFD) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) agonists (Zhang et al., 2019a) induce dWAT expansion.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: dWAT has unique roles in skin fibrosis and scarring.
source: Recent studies have revealed unique roles for dWAT in skin fibrosis and scarring (Marangoni et al., 2015; Varga and Marangoni, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019b), wound healing (Plikus et al., 2017; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013; Shook et al., 2020), immune modulation (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), and regeneration of hair follicles (Donati et al., 2014; Festa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: dWAT has unique roles in wound healing.
source: Recent studies have revealed unique roles for dWAT in skin fibrosis and scarring (Marangoni et al., 2015; Varga and Marangoni, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019b), wound healing (Plikus et al., 2017; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013; Shook et al., 2020), immune modulation (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), and regeneration of hair follicles (Donati et al., 2014; Festa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: dWAT has unique roles in immune modulation.
source: Recent studies have revealed unique roles for dWAT in skin fibrosis and scarring (Marangoni et al., 2015; Varga and Marangoni, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019b), wound healing (Plikus et al., 2017; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013; Shook et al., 2020), immune modulation (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), and regeneration of hair follicles (Donati et al., 2014; Festa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: dWAT has unique roles in regeneration of hair follicles.
source: Recent studies have revealed unique roles for dWAT in skin fibrosis and scarring (Marangoni et al., 2015; Varga and Marangoni, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019b), wound healing (Plikus et al., 2017; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013; Shook et al., 2020), immune modulation (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), and regeneration of hair follicles (Donati et al., 2014; Festa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dermal adipose tissue expands in the anagen phase and regresses in catagen phase during the hair cycle.
source: During the hair cycle, dermal adipose tissue expands in the anagen phase and regresses in catagen phase, providing vital signals to regulate hair growth (Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The reduction in dWAT in transgenic and pharmacologically treated mice results in a scaly skin phenotype with delayed hair coat formation, poorly developed pilosebaceous structures and epidermal barrier function.
source: In addition, the reduction in dWAT in transgenic and pharmacologically treated mice results in a scaly skin phenotype with delayed hair coat formation, poorly developed pilosebaceous structures and epidermal barrier function (Chen et al., 2002; Herrmann et al., 2003), and these phenomena resembled the abnormalities in skin observed upon EGFR inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dermal adipocytes surrounding the site of skin injury undergo lipolysis and dedifferentiation, transition to myofibroblasts and attract macrophages to stimulate re-epithelialization and revascularization.
source: Dermal adipocytes surrounding the site of skin injury undergo lipolysis and dedifferentiation, transition to myofibroblasts and attract macrophages to stimulate re-epithelialization and revascularization (Shook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: New adipocytes regenerating from myofibroblasts were observed in healed wounds.
source: Additionally, new adipocytes regenerating from myofibroblasts were also observed in healed wounds (Plikus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The importance of dWAT in host defense is the promotion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (Camp) release during adipogenic differentiation.
source: The importance of dWAT in host defense is the promotion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (Camp) release during adipogenic differentiation (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The production of Camp defends against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infection.
source: The production of Camp defends against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infection, which often develops along with EGFRI skin toxicities (Lichtenberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: S. aureus infection often develops along with EGFRI skin toxicities.
source: The production of Camp defends against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) infection, which often develops along with EGFRI skin toxicities (Lichtenberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Rats continued losing weight throughout the Afa intervention.
source: Rats continued losing weight and exhibited reduced food intake throughout the Afa intervention, and at the end of the treatment, they had lost up to 27.9% and 23.1% of their initial body weight and food intake, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the rat model experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Rats exhibited reduced food intake throughout the Afa intervention.
source: Rats continued losing weight and exhibited reduced food intake throughout the Afa intervention, and at the end of the treatment, they had lost up to 27.9% and 23.1% of their initial body weight and food intake, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the rat model experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At the end of Afa treatment, rats had lost up to 27.9% of their initial body weight.
source: Rats continued losing weight and exhibited reduced food intake throughout the Afa intervention, and at the end of the treatment, they had lost up to 27.9% and 23.1% of their initial body weight and food intake, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the rat model experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At the end of Afa treatment, rats had lost up to 23.1% of their initial food intake.
source: Rats continued losing weight and exhibited reduced food intake throughout the Afa intervention, and at the end of the treatment, they had lost up to 27.9% and 23.1% of their initial body weight and food intake, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the rat model experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: After 3 days of Afa treatment, few rats began to develop skin lesions.
source: After 3 days of treatment, few rats began to occur the skin lesions, until day 7, almost all rats developed rash with 23.08% of them were grade two and above.
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the rat model experiment.

claim: By day 7 of Afa treatment, almost all rats developed rash with 23.08% of them being grade two and above.
source: After 3 days of treatment, few rats began to occur the skin lesions, until day 7, almost all rats developed rash with 23.08% of them were grade two and above.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the rat model experiment.

claim: Grade three rash happened at day eight and increased in the next two days.
source: Grade three rash happened at day eight and increased in the next two days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a temporal observation from the rat model experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The rat model recapitulated all skin features of patients receiving EGFRIs, including erythema, pustules and itching.
source: The rat model recapitulated all skin features of patients receiving EGFRIs, including erythema, pustules and itching, and the pustules conflated to lakes of pus that dried and formed yellow crusts when rash developed to a higher grade (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a validation of the rat model, supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: Pustules conflated to lakes of pus that dried and formed yellow crusts when rash developed to a higher grade.
source: The rat model recapitulated all skin features of patients receiving EGFRIs, including erythema, pustules and itching, and the pustules conflated to lakes of pus that dried and formed yellow crusts when rash developed to a higher grade (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the rat model, supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: Administrations by other EGFRIs, such as Erlotinib, Gefitinib, Osimertinib, had similar phenotypes.
source: Administrations by other EGFRIs, such as Erlotinib, Gefitinib, Osimertinib, had similar phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding showing consistency across different EGFRIs, supported by visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a dense inflammatory infiltrate with a marked clustering of CD68+ macrophages, CD3+ T cells, CD11b+ immune cells, and mast cells in the dermis.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a dense inflammatory infiltrate with a marked clustering of CD68+ macrophages, CD3+ T cells, CD11b+ immune cells, and mast cells in the dermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Afa dramatically increased the expression of proinflammatory chemokines such as Ccl2, Ccl5, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3.
source: The cytokine expression file showed a similar tendency with human biopsies and mouse models (Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013), Afa dramatically increased the expression of proinflammatory chemokines such as Ccl2, Ccl5, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The cytokine expression profile showed a similar tendency with human biopsies and mouse models.
source: The cytokine expression file showed a similar tendency with human biopsies and mouse models (Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013), Afa dramatically increased the expression of proinflammatory chemokines such as Ccl2, Ccl5, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a comparative finding supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The thickness of the dWAT layer decreased with an increase in the rash grade.
source: The thickness of the dWAT layer decreased with an increase in the rash grade, and skin lipid levels also decreased (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Skin lipid levels decreased with an increase in the rash grade.
source: The thickness of the dWAT layer decreased with an increase in the rash grade, and skin lipid levels also decreased (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of cells stained with the adipocyte surface protein Caveolin-1 was observed.
source: A significant decrease in the number of cells stained with the adipocyte surface protein Caveolin-1 was also observed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Shaving-induced hair eruption has an important impact on rash progress during the EGFR inhibitor treatment.
source: A recent study described the importance of hair eruption on rash occurrence (Klufa et al., 2019). In our rat model, there was a similar situation that the skin rash occurred earlier and was more severe on shaved back skin than on the unshaved area (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B). This result indicates that shaving-induced hair eruption has an important impact on rash progress during the EGFR inhibitor treatment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The skin rash occurred earlier and was more severe on shaved back skin than on the unshaved area.
source: In our rat model, there was a similar situation that the skin rash occurred earlier and was more severe on shaved back skin than on the unshaved area (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the rat model, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The unshaved area still developed abnormal erythema.
source: The unshaved area still developed abnormal erythema (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and showed dWAT reduction after long-term Afa treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is an observation from the rat model, supported by visual evidence in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The unshaved area showed dWAT reduction after long-term Afa treatment.
source: The unshaved area still developed abnormal erythema (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and showed dWAT reduction after long-term Afa treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: The attenuation of intradermal adipocytes was due to a decrease in both size and number.
source: Changes in dWAT were examined by performing a detailed morphometric analysis. The attenuation of intradermal adipocytes was due to a decrease in both size and number, and time-course studies revealed that the size change occurred prior to the change in adipocyte number (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is a finding from morphometric analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: Time-course studies revealed that the size change occurred prior to the change in adipocyte number.
source: The attenuation of intradermal adipocytes was due to a decrease in both size and number, and time-course studies revealed that the size change occurred prior to the change in adipocyte number (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is a temporal finding from time-course analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: A positive correlation existed between dWAT thickness and rash grade throughout Afa treatment.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, a positive correlation existed between dWAT thickness and rash grade throughout Afa treatment (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a correlation finding supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: iWAT and BAT showed a decreasing trend at late time points.
source: Thus, we also monitored the weight change of sWAT and other skin adipose depots, and found that iWAT and BAT also showed a decreasing trend at late time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), whereas sWAT represented a more similar response to dWAT during rash occurrence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from weight monitoring, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: sWAT represented a more similar response to dWAT during rash occurrence.
source: Thus, we also monitored the weight change of sWAT and other skin adipose depots, and found that iWAT and BAT also showed a decreasing trend at late time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), whereas sWAT represented a more similar response to dWAT during rash occurrence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from weight monitoring, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: The expressions of general adipocyte marker genes were significantly decreased at the end of the treatment.
source: To examine whether the differentiation of dermal adipocyte was affected, we first compared the expression of differentiation-associated genes in Afa-treated skin with that in vehicle-treated skin using quantitative PCR. The expressions of general adipocyte marker genes were significantly decreased at the end of the treatment (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Reduced expression of PPARγ and Perilinpin-2 were detected in skin samples from rats.
source: Reduced expression of PPARγ and Perilinpin-2 were also detected in skin samples from rats (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: Rats receiving daily Afa treatments showed a time-dependent progressive decrease in dWAT thickness associated with a slightly thicker dermis and collagen deposition in the early stage of rash.
source: To characterize dermal adipocyte differentiation, we first performed Masson's trichrome staining for collagen to characterize dermal adipocyte differentiation. Rats receiving daily Afa treatments showed a time-dependent progressive decrease in dWAT thickness associated with a slightly thicker dermis and collagen deposition in the early stage of rash (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Dermal adipocytes isolated from the back skin of Afa-treated rats only exhibited slight fibrotic potential in the early stage that diminished quickly.
source: We next analyzed the expression of fibrotic genes in dWAT before and after rash to evaluate the adipocyte to fibroblast transdifferentiation process. However, dermal adipocytes isolated from the back skin of Afa-treated rats only exhibited slight fibrotic potential in the early stage that diminished quickly (Figure 2C), whereas the expression of general adipocyte markers represented a continuous and obvious decrease (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expression of general adipocyte markers represented a continuous and obvious decrease.
source: However, dermal adipocytes isolated from the back skin of Afa-treated rats only exhibited slight fibrotic potential in the early stage that diminished quickly (Figure 2C), whereas the expression of general adipocyte markers represented a continuous and obvious decrease (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Collagen deposition and myofibroblast transition occur in the early phases of EGFRI-related skin changes and are sustained for only a short period.
source: These data suggest that collagen deposition and myofibroblast transition occur in the early phases of EGFRI-related skin changes and are sustained for only a short period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Upon EGFRI stimulation, attached adipocytes began to decrease the size of lipid droplets and the cells formed spindle-like shapes on day four after Afa treatment.
source: To determine whether dedifferentiation exists, ceiling culture was performed using dWAT cells isolated from normal rat back skin. Upon EGFRI stimulation, we found that attached adipocytes began to decrease the size of lipid droplets and the cells formed spindle-like shapes on day four after Afa treatment.
evidence: This is a morphological observation from ceiling culture experiments.

claim: Adipocytes gradually elongated, lost intracellular lipids and proliferated as fully dedifferentiated PDGFRα + fibrocytes.
source: Then, they gradually elongated, lost intracellular lipids and proliferated as fully dedifferentiated PDGFRα + fibrocytes (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a morphological observation from ceiling culture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Adipocytes cultured under control experimental conditions attached much fewer and still retained lipid droplets.
source: In comparison, adipocytes cultured under control experimental conditions attached much fewer and still retained lipid droplets (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from ceiling culture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: Application of Rosi reversed the dedifferentiation of dermal adipocytes induced by Afa.
source: We evaluated the effect of Rosi on Afa-treated dermal adipocytes to directly test this hypothesis. Application of Rosi reversed the dedifferentiation of dermal adipocytes induced by Afa, and cells cultured in the presence of Rosi displayed little attachment until 14 days (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from ceiling culture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: Cells cultured in the presence of Rosi displayed little attachment until 14 days.
source: Application of Rosi reversed the dedifferentiation of dermal adipocytes induced by Afa, and cells cultured in the presence of Rosi displayed little attachment until 14 days (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from ceiling culture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2E–G.

claim: The transcriptional level of Pparg was downregulated by Afa and upregulated by Rosi.
source: Correspondingly, the transcriptional level of Pparg was downregulated by Afa and upregulated by Rosi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: An EGFR signaling deficiency, caused by treatment with EGFRI, triggers the dermal adipocyte-myofibroblast transition at an early stage and significant dedifferentiation.
source: In summary, these results suggest that an EGFR signaling deficiency, caused by treatment with EGFRI, triggers the dermal adipocyte-myofibroblast transition at an early stage and significant dedifferentiation, and the PPARγ agonist Rosi effectively rescues this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The PPARγ agonist Rosi effectively rescues the dermal adipocyte-myofibroblast transition and dedifferentiation.
source: In summary, these results suggest that an EGFR signaling deficiency, caused by treatment with EGFRI, triggers the dermal adipocyte-myofibroblast transition at an early stage and significant dedifferentiation, and the PPARγ agonist Rosi effectively rescues this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The differentiation of dFBs in the presence of Afa was inhibited.
source: To determine whether the loss of mature dWAT cells was caused by EGFR inhibition on APs, we isolated dFBs from the skin dermis and treated them with Afa for 3, 6 and 9 days during adipogenic differentiation in vitro. Consistent with our hypothesis, the differentiation of dFBs in the presence of Afa was inhibited (Figure 3A and B), and the concentration of Afa used in this experiment had little antiproliferative effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro differentiation assays, supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The concentration of Afa used in this experiment had little antiproliferative effect.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the differentiation of dFBs in the presence of Afa was inhibited (Figure 3A and B), and the concentration of Afa used in this experiment had little antiproliferative effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a control finding from cell viability assays, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The addition of Rosi circumvented the inhibition of adipogenic differentiation.
source: Notably, the addition of Rosi circumvented the inhibition of adipogenic differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro differentiation assays, supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The gene signature induced by Afa in APs was similar to the changes in gene expression observed in mature adipocytes.
source: Next, we aimed to define the molecular pathways affected by EGFR inhibition in dermal adipogenic cells. The gene signature induced by Afa in APs (Figure 3C) was similar to the changes in gene expression observed in mature adipocytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 2D.

claim: The expression levels of many pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors were increased during Afa treatment.
source: Adipocytes have been shown to express a variety of pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors, including TLR1-9, NOD1-2, TNFR, IL4R, and IL6R (Chen et al., 2019; Deiuliis et al., 2011; Sindhu et al., 2015). Interestingly, the expression levels of many of these receptors were increased during Afa treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating the proinflammatory potential of adipocytes upon EGFR inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Significantly increased levels of PDGFRα were detected on days 6 and 9, indicating a retardation of AP differentiation.
source: Additionally, we analyzed the levels of PDGFRα and phosphorylated AKT. Significantly increased levels of PDGFRα were detected on days 6 and 9, indicating a retardation of AP differentiation.
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis with an interpretation.

claim: Phospho-AKT1 and phospho-AKT2 levels were affected by Afa.
source: Phospho-AKT1 and phospho-AKT2 levels were also affected by Afa (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Cotreatment with the PPARγ agonist Rosi and the EGFR inhibitor Afa completely abrogated the inhibition of APs differentiation.
source: Cotreatment with the PPARγ agonist Rosi and the EGFR inhibitor Afa completely abrogated the inhibition of APs differentiation.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro differentiation assays.

claim: The addition of Rosi significantly activated both AKT1 and AKT2.
source: Notably, the addition of Rosi significantly activated both AKT1 and AKT2 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: APs (CD31-, CD45-, CD34+, CD29+) were absent after EGFR inhibition.
source: We next examined the number of APs in EGFRI-treated rats. Using FACS, we found that APs (CD31-, CD45-, CD34+, CD29+) were absent after EGFR inhibition (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The loss of mature dermal adipocytes induced by an EGFRI correlates with loss of APs and inhibition of their activation.
source: Together, these data indicate that the loss of mature dermal adipocytes induced by an EGFRI correlates with loss of APs and inhibition of their activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment of Afa resulted in increased S. aureus infection.
source: Since recent reports have shown that dermal adipocytes have the capacity to inhibit invasive bacterial skin infection and support hair regeneration (Festa et al., 2011; ), we determined whether the reduction and inhibition of APs contribute to the loss of these functions. As expected, treatment of Afa resulted in increased S. aureus infection (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from bacterial infection assays, supported by data shown in Figure 3H and citations to previous studies.

claim: The transcriptional level of Camp both in isolated dWAT and differentiated dFB were decreased by Afa.
source: To verify the relationship between Afa-induced dWAT reduction and S. aureus infection, we performed transcriptional experiments of dermal adipocyte cells. Correspondingly, the transcriptional level of Camp both in isolated dWAT (Figure 3I) and differentiated dFB (Figure 3J) were decreased by Afa, and Rosi significantly upregulated the expression level (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3J.

claim: Rosi significantly upregulated the expression level of Camp.
source: Correspondingly, the transcriptional level of Camp both in isolated dWAT (Figure 3I) and differentiated dFB (Figure 3J) were decreased by Afa, and Rosi significantly upregulated the expression level (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The number of hair follicles in anagen phase decreased with an increasing rash grade.
source: In addition, the number of hair follicles in anagen phase decreased with an increasing rash grade (Figure 3K), and rats treated with the EGFRI showed hair follicles with abnormal growth (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Rats treated with the EGFRI showed hair follicles with abnormal growth.
source: In addition, the number of hair follicles in anagen phase decreased with an increasing rash grade (Figure 3K), and rats treated with the EGFRI showed hair follicles with abnormal growth (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The levels of phospho-EGFR and ERK in dWAT and the outer sheath of hair follicles were significantly decreased.
source: The levels of phospho-EGFR and ERK in dWAT and the outer sheath of hair follicles were significantly decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of proliferative cells characterized by Ki67 immunostaining was reduced.
source: Consequently, the number of proliferative cells characterized by Ki67 immunostaining was reduced, and the number of apoptotic cells detected using TUNEL immunofluorescence staining was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The number of apoptotic cells detected using TUNEL immunofluorescence staining was increased.
source: Consequently, the number of proliferative cells characterized by Ki67 immunostaining was reduced, and the number of apoptotic cells detected using TUNEL immunofluorescence staining was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: A lack of APs and mature dWAT might contribute to impairing the maintenance of the host defense and hair growth in the skin.
source: Therefore, our results showed that a lack of APs and mature dWAT might contribute to impairing the maintenance of the host defense and hair growth in the skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Increased levels of ATGL and pHSL were observed in dWAT.
source: To examine whether lipolysis occurs after EGFR inhibition, isolated dermal adipocytes were assessed using transmission electron microscopy, and the expression of lipolysis-activated markers, the rate-limiting enzyme ATGL and phosphorylated hormone-sensitive lipase (pHSL) were detected. We observed increased levels of ATGL and pHSL in dWAT (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Multiple smaller droplets adjacent to large lipid droplets were detected in Afa-treated rats, whereas only large, unilocular lipids were retained in the control group.
source: Consistent with these changes, multiple smaller droplets adjacent to large lipid droplets were detected in Afa-treated rats, whereas only large, unilocular lipids were retained in the control group (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from transmission electron microscopy, supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In sWAT, lipolysis-induced glycerol production was not increased in either sWAT isolated from Afa-treated rats or Afa stimulation of sWAT from Ctrl-treated rats.
source: However, in sWAT, lipolysis-induced glycerol production was not increase in either sWAT isolated from Afa-treated rats or Afa stimulation of sWAT from Ctrl-treated rats (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from lipolysis assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The fatty acid composition of adipocytes from Afa- or Ctrl-treated rats did not show any significant differences, and the only significantly changed medium-chain FA was decanoic acid (10:0).
source: We performed lipidomics on isolated dermal adipocytes from Ctrl- or Afa-treated rats to characterize the composition of fatty acids (FAs). The fatty acid composition of adipocytes from Afa- or Ctrl-treated rats did not show any significant differences, and the only significantly changed medium-chain FA was decanoic acid (10:0) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from lipidomics analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The most abundant FAs were mainly C18 fatty acids, including methyl oleate (18:1), methyl elaidate (18:1T), methyl linoleate (18:2) and methyl linoelaidate (18:2T).
source: Notably, the most abundant FAs were mainly C18 fatty acids, including methyl oleate (18:1), methyl elaidate (18:1T), methyl linoleate (18:2) and methyl linoelaidate (18:2T) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), indicating the extensive release of these types of FAs to the cell matrix during lipolysis.
evidence: This is a finding from lipidomics analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The free fatty acid (FFA) in the skin homogenates showed an enrichment in Afa-treated rats.
source: Correspondingly, the free fatty acid (FFA) in the skin homogenates showed an enrichment in Afa-treated rats (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from FFA assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lipolysis and a decrease in adipocyte size corresponded with the infiltration of macrophages when rash occurred.
source: Experimental studies support the hypothesis that lipolysis-induced lipid accumulation drives macrophage infiltration (Kosteli et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2006). Lipolysis and a decrease in adipocyte size corresponded with the infiltration of macrophages when rash occurred (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4D and E and citations to previous studies.

claim: The number of migrated monocytes was increased in the 18:2-treated wells.
source: We hypothesized that individual FA components might promote the migration of macrophages. Monocytes have been well known migrated to local inflammatory sites and differentiated to macrophages. Thus, we treated human monocyte THP-1 cells with one significantly changed FA, decanoic acid (10:0), or the other four most abundant C18 FAs to verify this hypothesis. In particular, we observed that the number of migrated monocytes was increased in the 18:2-treated wells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is a finding from migration assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Direct treatment of adipocytes with Afa did not increase lipase expression or lipolysis-induced glycerol production.
source: To further study how EGFR inhibition promotes adipocyte lipolysis, we performed a direct EGFRI treatment on dFB-derived adipocytes. Unexpectedly, direct treatment of adipocytes with Afa did not increase lipase expression or lipolysis-induced glycerol production (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro lipolysis assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Treatment of adipocytes by homogenates from rat skin revealed obvious upregulation of lipase activity.
source: However, treatment of adipocytes by homogenates from rat skin revealed obvious upregulation of lipase activity (Figure 4F), thus indicating that cytokines secreted by other skin cells might contribute to lipolysis.
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Afa-stimulated HaCaT cells exhibited higher expression levels of IL6, but not TNFα.
source: We doubted whether epidermal HaCaT cells regulated adipose lipolysis by releasing inflammatory cytokines. Consistent with previous findings, Afa-stimulated HaCaT cells exhibited higher expression levels of IL6, but not TNFα (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The addition of Rosi exerted an obvious inhibitory effect on the transcription of IL6.
source: Notably, the addition of Rosi exerted an obvious inhibitory effect on the transcription of IL6 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Multiple small lipid droplets formed in the Afa-treated dFB, while larger lipids maintained in the Ctrl group.
source: First, we added Afa to epidermal HaCaT cells to stimulate IL6 transcription, then treated differentiated-dFBs with the supernatants from HaCaT cells, and finally collected dFB supernatants for monocyte chemotactic assays. Multiple small lipid droplets formed in the Afa-treated dFB, while larger lipids maintained in the Ctrl group (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from coculture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The number of migrated monocytes was significantly increased in the Afa group.
source: The number of migrated monocytes was also significantly increased in the Afa group (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: This is a finding from migration assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: Addition of Rosi simultaneously with Afa suppressed both the lipolysis and monocyte migration.
source: Notably, addition of Rosi simultaneously with Afa suppressed both the lipolysis and monocyte migration (Figure 4I–K), indicating that the production of inflammatory cytokines was inhibited by Rosi at the initial stage.
evidence: This is a finding from coculture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4I–K.

claim: Secreted IL6 was increased after Afa treatment both in rat skin homogenates and HaCaT supernatants, and decreased with the addition of Rosi.
source: Consistent with the transcriptional level, secreted IL6 was increased after Afa treatment both in rat skin homogenates and HaCaT supernatants, and decreased with the addition of Rosi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L).
evidence: This is a finding from ELISA assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L.

claim: The IL6 secreted by keratinocytes induced lipolysis of adipocytes.
source: We next performed the stimulation of IL6 on differentiated-dFB, the lipolysis enhanced by increased level of lipase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), suggesting that the IL6 secreted by keratinocytes induced lipolysis of adipocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M.

claim: Treatment of adipocytes with Rosi in the presence of supernatant from Afa-treated HaCaT cells improved lipid stability.
source: To evaluate the direct effect of Rosi on adipocytes during lipolysis, we treated adipocytes with Rosi in the presence of supernatant from Afa-treated HaCaT cells. The lipid stability was improved with the existence of Rosi (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is a finding from coculture experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The elevated chemotaxis of monocytes was attenuated by Rosi.
source: Although not as significant as the results shown in Figure 4J and K, the elevated chemotaxis of monocytes was also attenuated by Rosi (Figure 4M and N).
evidence: This is a finding from migration assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4M and N.

claim: The induction of inflammation was remarkable in differentiated dFBs compared with stimulation of undifferentiated dFBs.
source: Given the importance of lipolysis in inflammation, we then dissected whether the participation of adipocytes amplified the inflammatory response. Compared with stimulation of undifferentiated dFBs, the induction of inflammation was remarkable in differentiated dFBs (Figure 4O and P).
evidence: This is a finding from migration assays, supported by data shown in Figure 4O and P.

claim: The EGFRI induced dermal adipocyte lipolysis, whereas the production of lipolytic cytokines was not induced by the direct stimulation of adipocytes but occurred in keratinocytes.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the EGFRI induced dermal adipocyte lipolysis, whereas the production of lipolytic cytokines was not induced by the direct stimulation of adipocytes but occurred in keratinocytes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The increased levels of FAs, especially 18:2, are likely to induce monocyte migration.
source: The increased levels of FAs, especially 18:2, are likely to induce monocyte migration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rosi treatment alleviated lipolysis and the inflammatory response by acting on both the epidermis and adipocytes.
source: Rosi treatment alleviated lipolysis and the inflammatory response by acting on both the epidermis and adipocytes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Rats fed an HFD for 5 weeks showed an expansion of the dermal adipose layer and a significant increase in the adipocyte size.
source: To weaken the metabolic disorders in the obese state, we administered a short-term HFD diet and subsequent EGFRI treatment. Rats fed an HFD for 5 weeks showed an expansion of the dermal adipose layer and a significant increase in the adipocyte size (Figure 5A–C), while no differences were observed in other adipose depots (Figure 5D), body weight changes (Figure 5E) or systemic serum lipid levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the HFD experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: No differences were observed in other adipose depots, body weight changes or systemic serum lipid levels after 5 weeks of HFD feeding.
source: Rats fed an HFD for 5 weeks showed an expansion of the dermal adipose layer and a significant increase in the adipocyte size (Figure 5A–C), while no differences were observed in other adipose depots (Figure 5D), body weight changes (Figure 5E) or systemic serum lipid levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the HFD experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5D, Figure 5E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Significant increases in adipogenesis and AKT phosphorylation were observed in dFB of rats after 5 weeks of HFD feeding.
source: We analyzed the expression of general adipogenic genes and AKT signaling in the dFB of rats after 5 weeks of HFD feeding to examine whether AP activation was increased. Significant increases in adipogenesis and AKT phosphorylation were observed (Figure 5F and G), verifying an increase in adipogenic ability stimulated by the HFD.
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot and gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The HFD group showed a reduced occurrence and exacerbation of rash.
source: Notably, the HFD group showed a reduced occurrence and exacerbation of rash (Figure 5H and I; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the HFD experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5H and I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rats fed an HFD displayed lower white blood cell, granulocyte and lymphocyte percentages.
source: This result is consistent with a thicker dermal adipose layer and abundant lipid staining (Figure 5J). In addition, rats fed an HFD displayed lower white blood cell, granulocyte and lymphocyte percentages (Supplementary file 2), the skin infiltration of various immune cells, including mast cell, macrophage, T cell, and monocyte were also decreased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from blood analysis, supported by data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The skin infiltration of various immune cells, including mast cell, macrophage, T cell, and monocyte were decreased in rats fed an HFD.
source: In addition, rats fed an HFD displayed lower white blood cell, granulocyte and lymphocyte percentages (Supplementary file 2), the skin infiltration of various immune cells, including mast cell, macrophage, T cell, and monocyte were also decreased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of inflammatory receptors and their ligands were lower in HFD-treated rats than that in Ctrl-treated rats, suggesting a reduced inflammatory response.
source: The expression of inflammatory receptors and their ligands were also lower than that in Ctrl-treated rats, suggesting a reduced inflammatory response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression and immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: The ablation of dWAT resulted in a moderate deterioration in rash severity after 8 days.
source: After dWAT ablation, we examined the skin rash process induced by Afa oral gavage in control and DCA rats. The ablation of dWAT didn't affect body weight or food intake (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, G), but resulted in a moderate deterioration in rash severity after 8 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H-J).
evidence: This is a finding from the DCA ablation experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H-J.

claim: The ablation of dWAT didn't affect body weight or food intake.
source: The ablation of dWAT didn't affect body weight or food intake (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, G), but resulted in a moderate deterioration in rash severity after 8 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H-J).
evidence: This is a finding from the DCA ablation experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F, G.

claim: Dermal adipocytes exert potent protective effects on maintaining skin homoeostasis during EGFR inhibition.
source: Taken together, we conclude that dermal adipocytes exert potent protective effects on maintaining skin homoeostasis during EGFR inhibition, and the expansion of dWAT is an effective intervention to attenuate skin toxicities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HFD and DCA experiments.

claim: The expansion of dWAT is an effective intervention to attenuate skin toxicities.
source: Taken together, we conclude that dermal adipocytes exert potent protective effects on maintaining skin homoeostasis during EGFR inhibition, and the expansion of dWAT is an effective intervention to attenuate skin toxicities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HFD and DCA experiments.

claim: Modulating dWAT by the topical application of Rosi gel caused obvious improvements in skin phenotypes.
source: We topically applied a Rosi gel and its vehicle gel on shaved backs of rats daily after Afa gavage to assess the prophylactic effect of Rosi on skin toxicity during Afa treatment. Modulating dWAT by the topical application of Rosi gel caused obvious improvements in skin phenotypes (Figure 6A), with a delayed process and low occurrence of rash (Figure 6B and C), and improvements in body weight changes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the topical Rosi application experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Topical application of Rosi gel resulted in a delayed process and low occurrence of rash.
source: Modulating dWAT by the topical application of Rosi gel caused obvious improvements in skin phenotypes (Figure 6A), with a delayed process and low occurrence of rash (Figure 6B and C), and improvements in body weight changes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the topical Rosi application experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Topical application of Rosi gel resulted in improvements in body weight changes.
source: Modulating dWAT by the topical application of Rosi gel caused obvious improvements in skin phenotypes (Figure 6A), with a delayed process and low occurrence of rash (Figure 6B and C), and improvements in body weight changes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the topical Rosi application experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The architecture of Rosi-treated skin showed fewer neutrophil microcysts, less vascular dilatation and congestion, and more parallel growing hair follicles in anagen phase.
source: The architecture of Rosi-treated skin showed fewer neutrophil microcysts, less vascular dilatation and congestion, and more parallel growing hair follicles in anagen phase (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: The dermal adipocyte layer was still retained in the Rosi group.
source: Specifically, the dermal adipocyte layer was still retained in the Rosi group (Figure 6E and H).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6E and H.

claim: The adipogenic ability recovered after Rosi treatment.
source: The adipogenic ability recovered (Figure 6I; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and lipolysis decreased after Rosi treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression and immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lipolysis decreased after Rosi treatment.
source: The adipogenic ability recovered (Figure 6I; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and lipolysis decreased after Rosi treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of APs increased after Rosi treatment.
source: Consistent with our previous investigations, the number of APs increased after Rosi treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D), accompanied by an increased ability to defend against S. aureus (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Rosi treatment resulted in an increased ability to defend against S. aureus.
source: Consistent with our previous investigations, the number of APs increased after Rosi treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D), accompanied by an increased ability to defend against S. aureus (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a finding from bacterial infection assays, supported by data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The application of Rosi improved serum lipid levels.
source: Additionally, the application of Rosi also improved serum lipid levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from serum lipid analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increased expression level of inflammatory cytokines was downregulated after Rosi treatment.
source: The increased expression level of inflammatory cytokines was downregulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and the immune infiltration was attenuated obviously in Rosi-treated group (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The immune infiltration was attenuated obviously in Rosi-treated group.
source: The increased expression level of inflammatory cytokines was downregulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), and the immune infiltration was attenuated obviously in Rosi-treated group (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: The rash severity and body weight loss were both significantly alleviated by therapeutic treatment of Rosi.
source: To further verify Rosi's efficacy under therapeutic treatment setting, we applied Vehicle or Rosi gel after rats developed Grade one rash, the rash severity and body weight lose were both significantly alleviated by therapeutic treatment of Rosi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) compared with vehicle treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the therapeutic Rosi application experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tumor volumes decreased significantly in both the vehicle gel and Rosi gel groups after gavage of Afa.
source: We topically applied Rosi gel to nude mice subcutaneously receiving PC9 lung carcinoma cells, for which EGFR inhibitors are approved for first-line treatment. After the gavage of Afa, tumor volumes decreased significantly in both the vehicle gel and Rosi gel groups, and the tumor inhibition rates showed no change between vehicle and Rosi groups; in contrast, control mice treated with vehicle displayed rapid tumor growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-D).
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor xenograft experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: The tumor inhibition rates showed no change between vehicle and Rosi groups.
source: After the gavage of Afa, tumor volumes decreased significantly in both the vehicle gel and Rosi gel groups, and the tumor inhibition rates showed no change between vehicle and Rosi groups; in contrast, control mice treated with vehicle displayed rapid tumor growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-D).
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor xenograft experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Rosi improved body weight and tolerance to Afa.
source: Intriguingly, Rosi improved body weight and tolerance to Afa (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E), and mortality occurred in the Ctrl and Afa groups, with six mice in each group.
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor xenograft experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Rosi regulates dWAT to ameliorate EGFRI-associated cutaneous toxicity without interfering with the antitumor effect.
source: Taken together, these results clearly show that Rosi regulates dWAT to ameliorate EGFRI-associated cutaneous toxicity without interfering with the antitumor effect.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The severity of rash is commonly considered a factor associated with a better prognosis.
source: Cutaneous toxicities induced by anti-EGFR therapy, in particular rash, are the most frequent adverse effects observed in patients with EGFR-mutant cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, breast cancer and colorectal cancer. The severity of rash is commonly considered a factor associated with a better prognosis (Peréz-Soler and Saltz, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mice lacking EGFR in the epidermis developed the same phenotypes of skin lesions as patients treated with EGFRIs: neutrophilic pustules, initial infiltration of macrophages and mast cells, subsequent T cell infiltration, hair follicle destruction, keratin plugs and bacterial invasion.
source: Several epidermis-targeted genetic mouse models have revealed the relationship of epidermal EGFR with local immune cell activation, keratinocyte differentiation, hair eruption and microbiota outgrowth (Klufa et al., 2019; Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013; Satoh et al., 2020). Mice lacking EGFR in the epidermis developed the same phenotypes of skin lesions as patients treated with EGFRIs: neutrophilic pustules, initial infiltration of macrophages and mast cells, subsequent T cell infiltration, hair follicle destruction, keratin plugs and bacterial invasion (Mascia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In humans and mice, the recruitment of inflammatory cells is attributed to the production of proinflammatory chemokines such as CCL5 and CCL2.
source: In humans and mice, the recruitment of inflammatory cells is attributed to the production of proinflammatory chemokines such as CCL5 and CCL2 (Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Crossing EGFRΔep mice with CCR2-/-, MyD88-/-, TNFR-/- or NOS2-/- mice did not ameliorate the skin phenotype.
source: However, crossing EGFRΔep mice with CCR2-/-, MyD88-/-, TNFR-/- or NOS2-/- mice did not ameliorate the skin phenotype, while the depletion of macrophages or mast cells only slightly improved the skin phenotype (Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The depletion of macrophages or mast cells only slightly improved the skin phenotype.
source: However, crossing EGFRΔep mice with CCR2-/-, MyD88-/-, TNFR-/- or NOS2-/- mice did not ameliorate the skin phenotype, while the depletion of macrophages or mast cells only slightly improved the skin phenotype (Lichtenberger et al., 2013; Mascia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction in dermal adipocytes is an early response to EGFR inhibition and leads to the disorder of cutaneous homeostasis.
source: Here, we show that a reduction in dermal adipocytes is an early response to EGFR inhibition and leads to the disorder of cutaneous homeostasis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, supported by the schematic in Figure 7.

claim: Impaired adipogenesis decreased the skin defense against S. aureus, as well as the signaling interactions with hair follicles.
source: Impaired adipogenesis decreased the skin defense against S. aureus, as well as the signaling interactions with hair follicles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Activation of lipolysis in dermal fat occurs as a response to skin wound repair.
source: In addition, increased migration of monocytes was associated with lipolysis in adipocytes characterized by increased lipase activity. Activation of lipolysis in dermal fat occurs as a response to skin wound repair (Schmidt and Horsley, 2013; Shook et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages recruited during wound healing by lipolysis were reported to promote revascularization and re-epithelialization.
source: Although macrophages recruited during wound healing by lipolysis were reported to promote revascularization and re-epithelialization (Shook et al., 2020), increased macrophage numbers and free fatty acid contents may also stimulate inflammatory responses via various pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors in adipocytes, subsequently inducing cytokine expression and increasing chemoattractant activity (Shi et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased macrophage numbers and free fatty acid contents may stimulate inflammatory responses via various pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors in adipocytes, subsequently inducing cytokine expression and increasing chemoattractant activity.
source: Although macrophages recruited during wound healing by lipolysis were reported to promote revascularization and re-epithelialization (Shook et al., 2020), increased macrophage numbers and free fatty acid contents may also stimulate inflammatory responses via various pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors in adipocytes, subsequently inducing cytokine expression and increasing chemoattractant activity (Shi et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The infiltration of macrophages in adipose tissue coincided with circulating FFA concentrations and adipose lipolysis.
source: The infiltration of macrophages in adipose tissue coincided with circulating FFA concentrations and adipose lipolysis, and pharmacologically induced lipolysis by a β3-adrenergic agonist increased macrophage accumulation (Kosteli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Pharmacologically induced lipolysis by a β3-adrenergic agonist increased macrophage accumulation.
source: The infiltration of macrophages in adipose tissue coincided with circulating FFA concentrations and adipose lipolysis, and pharmacologically induced lipolysis by a β3-adrenergic agonist increased macrophage accumulation (Kosteli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Dermal adipocytes amplified inflammatory responses from epithelial cells primed with EGFRI treatment.
source: Notably, we showed that dermal adipocytes amplified inflammatory responses from epithelial cells primed with EGFRI treatment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The ability of dermal lipids to costimulate keratinocyte-generated cellular responses represents a novel pathway for the amplification of innate immunity and inflammation.
source: The ability of dermal lipids to costimulate keratinocyte-generated cellular responses represents a novel pathway for the amplification of innate immunity and inflammation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Local lipid fluxes are central regulators of the inflammatory response in EGFRI-affected dermal adipose tissue.
source: Based on these data, local lipid fluxes are central regulators of the inflammatory response in EGFRI-affected dermal adipose tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The dermal adipose layer is distinct from subcutaneous adipocytes and has a unique role in skin modulation.
source: In this study, we also found a distinction between dermal and subcutaneous white adipose tissue. Although both of these tissues respond early and decrease in size after EGFR inhibition, the expression of adipogenic and fibrotic genes shows different trends; additionally, lipolysis does not occur in subcutaneous fat. These results indicate that the dermal adipose layer is distinct from subcutaneous adipocytes and has a unique role in skin modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Innate immunity of dermal adipose tissue mediated by the release of antimicrobial peptides protects many organs from bacterial infection, such as the skin, peritoneum, endocardium and colon.
source: Innate immunity of dermal adipose tissue mediated by the release of antimicrobial peptides protects many organs from bacterial infection, such as the skin, peritoneum, endocardium and colon (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Impaired adipogenesis induced by the PPARγ inhibitors GW9662 and BADGE results in an increased bacterial infection in the skin and colon.
source: Impaired adipogenesis induced by the PPARγ inhibitors GW9662 and BADGE results in an increased bacterial infection in the skin and colon (Dokoshi et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retinoids enhance and sustain Camp levels in developing preadipocytes.
source: Moreover, a recent study observed that retinoids enhance and sustain Camp levels in developing preadipocytes (Liggins et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Retinoids are therapeutically useful against acne, a disorder driven partly by bacteria.
source: Interestingly, retinoids are therapeutically useful against acne, a disorder driven partly by bacteria (Chivot, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Scarring alopecia is caused by a specific Pparg depletion in hair follicle stem cells.
source: Another skin-related disorder called scarring alopecia is caused by a specific Pparg depletion in hair follicle stem cells, and immunohistochemical staining showed proinflammatory lipid and cell accumulation (Karnik et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Follicular stem cell activation was verified to be associated with dermal adipocytes.
source: The interplay between dWAT and hair follicles also involves the modulation of the stem cell niche. Follicular stem cell activation was verified to be associated with dermal adipocytes, and hair follicles of mice treated with BADGE or GW9662 did not enter anagen phase and were blocked in telogen phase (Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hair follicles of mice treated with BADGE or GW9662 did not enter anagen phase and were blocked in telogen phase.
source: Follicular stem cell activation was verified to be associated with dermal adipocytes, and hair follicles of mice treated with BADGE or GW9662 did not enter anagen phase and were blocked in telogen phase (Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PPARγ acts directly to negatively regulate the expression of inflammatory genes in a ligand-dependent manner by antagonizing the activities of transcription factors, such as members of the NF-κB and AP-1 families.
source: PPARγ acts directly to negatively regulate the expression of inflammatory genes in a ligand-dependent manner by antagonizing the activities of transcription factors, such as members of the NF-κB and AP-1 families.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of PPARγ action.

claim: PPARγ stimulation in rodents has been shown to ameliorate several inflammatory diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and acne vulgaris.
source: PPARγ stimulation in rodents has been shown to ameliorate several inflammatory diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and acne vulgaris (Ramot et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Topical application of rosiglitazone to EGFRI-treated rats prevents the onset of rash and ameliorates the symptoms.
source: Here, we show that dWAT plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of cutaneous toxicities induced by EGFR inhibition. Experiments with HFD feeding and DCA injection have shown that dWAT is required to maintain skin homeostasis during EGFR inhibition. Indeed, topical application of rosiglitazone to EGFRI-treated rats prevents the onset of rash and ameliorates the symptoms.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Topical application of rosiglitazone gel did not alter the antitumor effect of afatinib.
source: Additionally, based on the results obtained from the tumor-bearing nude mice, topical application of rosiglitazone gel did not alter the antitumor effect of afatinib.
evidence: This is a finding from the tumor xenograft experiment.

claim: PPARγ agonists may represent a promising new therapeutic strategy in the treatment of EGFRI-related skin disorders.
source: Therefore, PPARγ agonists may represent a promising new therapeutic strategy in the treatment of EGFRI-related skin disorders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.
